title: Cheese
wiki_lead:
Cheese is a type of dairy product produced in a range of flavors, textures, and forms by curdling of milk, usually from cows, goats or sheep, and sometimes of water buffalo. During production, milk is usually acidified and either the enzymes of rennet or bacterial enzymes with similar activity are added to cause the protein casein to coagulate. The solid curds, consisting of proteins and milkfat, are then separated from the liquid whey and pressed into finished cheese. Some cheeses have aromatic molds on the outer layer or rind, while others have them throughout.
Over a thousand types of cheese exist, produced in various countries. Their styles, textures and flavors depend on the origin of the milk (including the animal's diet), whether they have been pasteurised, the butterfat content, the bacteria and mold, the processing, and how long they have been aged. Herbs, spices, or wood smoke may be used as flavoring agents. Other added ingredients may include black pepper, garlic, chives or cranberries. A cheesemonger, or specialist seller of cheeses, may have expertise with selecting, purchasing, receiving, storing and ripening cheeses.
Most cheeses are acidified by bacteria, which turn milk sugars into lactic acid; the addition of rennet completes the curdling. Vegetarian varieties of rennet are available; most are produced through fermentation by the fungus Mucor miehei, but others have been extracted from Cynara thistles. For a few cheeses, the milk is curdled by adding acids such as vinegar or lemon juice.
Cheese is valued for its portability, long shelf life, and high content of fat, protein, calcium, and phosphorus. Cheese is more compact and has a longer shelf life than milk. Hard cheeses, such as Cheddar and Parmesan, last longer than soft cheeses, such as Brie or goat's milk cheese. The long storage life of some cheeses, especially when encased in a protective rind, allows producers to sell when markets are favourable. Vacuum packaging of block-shaped cheeses and gas-flushing of plastic bags with mixtures of carbon dioxide and nitrogen are used for storage and mass distribution of cheeses in the 21st century, compared with the paper and twine that was used in the 20th and 19th century.
A cheesemonger is a tradesperson who specializes in cheese by selling, curating, and caring for it.

Etymology
The word cheese comes from Latin caseus, from which the modern word casein is derived. The earliest source is the conjectured proto-Indo-European root *kwat-, which means "to ferment, become sour". That gave rise to cīese or cēse (in Old English) and chese (in Middle English).


History


Origins
The origins of cheese predate recorded history. There is no conclusive evidence indicating where cheesemaking originated, whether in Europe, Central Asia or the Middle East. The earliest proposed dates for the origin of cheesemaking range from around 8000 BCE, when sheep were first domesticated. Because animal skins and inflated internal organs have provided storage vessels for a range of foodstuffs since ancient times, it is probable that the process of cheese making was discovered accidentally by storing milk in a container made from the stomach of an animal, resulting in the milk being turned to curd and whey by the rennet from the stomach. There is a legend—with variations—about the discovery of cheese by an Arab trader who used this method of storing milk.
The earliest evidence of cheesemaking in the archaeological record dates back to 5500 BCE and is found in what is now Kuyavia, Poland, where strainers coated with milk-fat molecules have been found. The earliest evidence of cheesemaking in the Mediterranean dates back to 5200 BCE, on the coast of the Dalmatia region of Croatia.
Cheesemaking may have begun independently of this by the pressing and salting of curdled milk to preserve it. Observation that the effect of making cheese in an animal stomach gave more solid and better-textured curds may have led to the deliberate addition of rennet. 


Mesopotamia, Egypt and China
In Mesopotamian mythology, Inanna, goddess of fertility, love, the seasons and harvest, after wanting to marry Enkimdu, a farmer god, against her brother, sun god Utu's will, is petitioned by Dumuzi, the shepherd god, to marry him instead. In his petition Dumuzi compared between his own products: rich milk, yogurt, butter (or ghee) honey cheese and small cheeses, with those of the farmer: bread beans and dates, and concluded with the argument that he produces so much dairy that the human farmer could live off the surplus, Inanna was ultimately convinced and married Dumuzi. In another myth Inanna promised Dumuzi that she would preserve his storehouse in return for provisions of fresh milk, cream and cheese. As a result, cheese figured prominently in the long lived sacred marriage rite of the Dumuzi-Inanna cult, in which the king of Uruk, symbolizing Dumuzi, supplied Inanna, probably represented by a priestess, with cheese and cream, thereby securing her blessing for the following year. This rite was adopted by additional Sumerian cities such as Nippur, Ur and Isin, and evolved over time and place into different forms. It became the Akkadian sacred marriage rites between Nanna and Ningal, developed into that of Ningirsu and Bab, and Nanse and Nindar, and eventually into the Semitic-Akkadian rite of Tammuz-Ishtar which persisted into the common era. Numerous seals and tablets found in Inanna's temple serve as testimony to the annual quotas of cheese and butter herders were required to deliver to the goddess.
Early archeological evidence of Egyptian cheese has been found in Egyptian tomb murals, dating to about 2000 BCE. A 2018 scientific paper stated that cheese dating to approximately 1200 BCE was found in ancient Egyptian tombs. 
The earliest ever discovered preserved cheese was found on mummies in Xiaohe Cemetery in the Taklamakan Desert in Xinjiang, China, dating back as early as 1615 BCE.

grok_lead: Cheese is a dairy food produced from the coagulation and subsequent draining of milk, cream, skimmed milk, or partly skimmed milk, or combinations thereof, using suitable coagulants such as rennet or acid, resulting in a fresh or matured solid product. This process transforms liquid milk into a versatile food with diverse textures, flavors, and uses, ranging from fresh and soft varieties to aged and hard ones. The origins of cheese-making date back to the Neolithic period, with evidence of milk-fat residues in pottery from western Anatolia around the 7th millennium BCE and specialized ceramic sieves used for draining curds in Europe by 5500â5000 BCE. Early cheeses were likely soft, acid-coagulated products made from the milk of domesticated sheep and goats in the Fertile Crescent, developed as a way to preserve dairy for lactose-intolerant adults. By the 4th millennium BCE, proto-cuneiform tablets from Mesopotamia provide the first written records of cheese, and the practice spread with ancient civilizations, including Sumerians, Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, who refined techniques and documented over 100 varieties. In medieval Europe, monks advanced cheesemaking, preserving knowledge through monasteries, while the first commercial U.S. cheese factory opened in 1851 in New York, marking the shift to industrialized production. Today, cheese production consumes over one-third of U.S. milk supply, with natural cheese output exceeding 6 billion pounds annually since the 1990s. Cheese production begins with milk collection and preparation, often involving pasteurization to reduce pathogens, followed by the addition of starter cultures and coagulants to form curds. The curds are then cut, cooked, and drained to separate whey, after which saltingâeither dry or in brine âpreserves the product and develops flavor. The cheese is pressed into forms and aged under controlled conditions, with duration and environment varying by type; for instance, raw- milk cheeses require at least 60 days of aging at or above 2Â°C to ensure safety. Variations in milk type (cow, goat, sheep), coagulation method, temperature, and ripening introduce diversity: mesophilic cultures suit softer cheeses, while thermophilic ones yield harder varieties, and surface molds like Penicillium candidum create bloomy-rind types such as Camembert. There are over 1,000 known cheese varieties worldwide, broadly categorized into eight main types based on texture, moisture, and production method. Blue cheeses, like Gorgonzola (originating in Italy's Po Valley around 879 CE), feature veins from Penicillium molds and a pungent flavor. Hard cheeses, such as Parmesan, are low-moisture and aged for grating. Pasta filata types, including mozzarella, are stretched in hot water for elasticity. Processed cheeses are emulsified blends that melt smoothly. Semi-hard varieties like cheddar (ranging from mild creamy to sharp crumbly) balance firmness and flavor. Semi-soft options, such as Havarti, offer spreadable texture. Soft and fresh cheeses, like ricotta or cottage, are unaged and moist. Soft-ripened cheeses, including Brie, develop a runny interior under edible rinds. Nutritionally, cheese is dense in high-quality protein (about 8 grams per ounce of hard cheese), calcium (180 mg per ounce for bone health), and vitamins like B12 and A, while also providing probiotics in fermented varieties that may support gut and heart health. However, it is calorie-rich (around 120 calories per ounce of hard cheese) with high saturated fat (6 grams per ounce) and sodium (180â450 mg per serving), potentially raising risks for cardiovascular disease and hypertension if consumed excessively. Despite these concerns, moderate intakeâsuch as replacing red meat âhas been linked to lower stroke risk and no weight gain in some studies. Globally, cheese holds cultural significance in cuisines from French charcuterie to Italian pasta, with annual per capita consumption in the U.S. exceeding 40 pounds.
